title: Man dies after 'struggle' with Calgary police in hotel lobby, ASIRT investigating
subtitle: After officers attempted to de-escalate, a Taser was deployed, followed by pepper spray when he continued to be 'combative' toward police
article: A man has died after a "struggle" with Calgary police officers at a hotel on Macleod Trail early Tuesday morning, prompting an Alberta Serious Incident Response Team (ASIRT) investigation.

Around 12:55 a.m., Calgary police responded to reports of a man causing a disturbance and refusing to leave the Carriage House Hotel and Conference Centre at 9030 Macleod Tr. in the southwest community of Acadia.
Officers located a man in the lobby acting erratically upon arrival and attempted to de-escalate the situation, according to a Calgary Police Service release issued Tuesday .
"However, the man was not cooperative. A struggle ensued, resulting in one officer deploying a taser," police said.
The man continued to be "combative" with officers, resulting in one officer deploying OC spray (pepper spray).
The man was taken into custody and, shortly after, went into medical distress. Despite the efforts of EMS, he was declared deceased at the scene.
No one else was injured in the altercation.
At an unrelated press conference Tuesday afternoon Calgary police Chief Mark Neufeld, provided comments at a "high level," noting the ASIRT investigation is in its early stages.
"My thoughts are with the officers that are involved. For sure, it was a very harrowing experience, as well as the family of the individual who passed away," Neufeld said.
He did not provide any specific details of the incident, while the ASIRT investigation is continuing.

"Officers are trained to de-escalate situations in the best way that they can, some situations, though, are escalated by design, or they start out that way," Neufeld said. "So (it's) very difficult to sometimes de-escalate when people are struggling, whether it be with mental health or addictions or a combination thereof.
"Those will all be things worked out through the investigation."
He said calls which at first can appear to be innocuous can turn out to be dangerous.
"It just underscores that there's no such thing as a low-risk call - there's just unknown-risk calls," Neufeld said.
It's standard practice for ASIRT to investigate deaths of people while in police custody.
